Supports: the working definition of poverty as the state of lacking a usual or socially acceptable amount of money or material possessions, with poverty existing when people lack the means to satisfy basic needs; basic needs defined narrowly (survival) or broadly (the prevailing standard of living in the community) — the conceptual root of the absolute–relative distinction; the noneconomic connotations of the term (poor health, low skills, unwillingness to work, improvidence) and Britannica's warning that these obscure the inability to provide for basic needs; cyclical poverty (business-cycle fluctuations, mass unemployment in depressions and recessions) and collective poverty (underdevelopment, unequal distribution of wealth, generational transmission); and the general claim that the effects of poverty are harmful to both individuals and society. Facts synthesized; no source wording reproduced.

title: Folate - Health Professional Fact Sheet
notes: Read live 2026-08-22. Supports: folate is a water-soluble B vitamin naturally present in foods; folate is needed for DNA formation and cell division; megaloblastic anemia is the primary clinical sign of folate or vitamin B12 deficiency, with symptoms including weakness, fatigue, and difficulty concentrating; spinach, liver, asparagus, and brussels sprouts are among the foods with the highest folate levels; folate sources include vegetables, fruits, beans, dairy, meat, poultry, and grains; enriched grain products have been fortified with folic acid since 1998.

title: Vitamin A and Carotenoids: Fact Sheet for Consumers
notes: Read live 2026-08-22. Supports: vitamin A is fat-soluble and naturally present in many foods; roles in normal vision, immune system, reproduction, and growth; preformed vitamin A in fish, organ meats (liver), dairy, and eggs; provitamin A carotenoids (beta-carotene) in plant foods; deficiency sign xerophthalmia (inability to see in low light, can lead to blindness); high intakes of preformed vitamin A, usually from supplements, can cause severe headache, blurred vision, nausea, dizziness, muscle aches, and coordination problems and, in pregnancy, birth defects; high beta-carotene intake turns skin yellow-orange but lacks the same toxicity.

title: Vitamin B12 - Health Professional Fact Sheet
notes: Read live 2026-08-22. Supports: natural food sources of vitamin B12 are limited to animal foods (meat, fish, poultry, dairy, eggs); the body stores about 1 to 5 mg (about 1,000 to 2,000 times a typical daily intake), so deficiency symptoms can take several years to appear; vitamin B12 deficiency can cause fatigue, neurological changes, and megaloblastic anemia.

title: Vitamin C - Health Professional Fact Sheet
notes: Read live 2026-08-22. Supports: vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is a water-soluble vitamin that humans cannot synthesize, making it an essential dietary component; it is required for collagen biosynthesis, and collagen plays a vital role in wound healing; insufficient vitamin C intake causes scurvy, characterized by fatigue or lassitude and connective tissue weakness; best sources are fruits and vegetables, especially citrus fruits, red and green peppers, kiwifruit, broccoli, strawberries, and brussels sprouts.

title: Vitamin D: Fact Sheet for Consumers
notes: Read live 2026-08-22. Supports: vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium, a main building block for strong bones, and helps protect against osteoporosis; muscles and nerves need it; the body makes vitamin D when bare skin is exposed to the sun and does not make it through a window; fatty fish (trout, salmon, tuna, mackerel) and fish liver oils are the best natural sources, with small amounts in beef liver, egg yolks, and cheese; deficiency causes rickets in children and osteomalacia (bone pain, muscle weakness) in teens and adults; high blood levels can cause nausea, vomiting, muscle weakness, confusion, and kidney stones, are almost always caused by excessive supplement intake, and the skin limits production so sun cannot cause excess.

title: Vitamin E: Fact Sheet for Consumers
notes: Read live 2026-08-22. Supports: vitamin E is a fat-soluble nutrient that acts as an antioxidant protecting cells from free-radical damage and boosts the immune system; best sources are vegetable oils (wheat germ, sunflower, safflower), corn and soybean oils, nuts (peanuts, hazelnuts, almonds), sunflower seeds, and green vegetables (spinach, broccoli); deficiency is very rare in healthy people and almost always linked to conditions in which fat is not properly digested or absorbed (Crohn's, cystic fibrosis); high supplement doses might increase the risk of bleeding and hemorrhagic stroke.

title: Vitamin K: Fact Sheet for Consumers
notes: Read live 2026-08-22. Supports: vitamin K is important for blood clotting and healthy bones; sources include green leafy vegetables (spinach, kale, broccoli, lettuce), vegetable oils, some fruits (blueberries, figs), meat, cheese, eggs, and soybeans; bacteria in the colon make some vitamin K the body can absorb; severe deficiency causes bruising and bleeding problems because blood takes longer to clot; deficiency is very rare in the United States.
